title: What is left after npx skills add
eyebrow: 2026-09-19 · rev D · argued edges audited, four moved to suspected (#96)
problem: The skills installer copies a skill into agents that are not Claude Code. The skill text names a slash command, a preview pane, and a Windows command that another agent does not have. The renderer is a Node script inside the skill. A reader without the skill cannot render a box. This box decides what the text says, what the repository ships, and what the README tells a stranger first.
who: A reader who installs the skill into an agent that is not Claude Code.
when: Before the README told a stranger what to run, and the author settled it on 2026-08-26.

dims.name: How much Claude Code the text keeps
dims.question: The skill names Claude Code things. Do they stay?
dims.problem: The skill text names a slash command, an in-app preview pane, an Artifact tool, and a Windows command that opens a file. An agent that is not Claude Code has none of the first three. Four lines carry all of it. The skill now installs into many agents, so a reader who cannot follow an instruction learns to skip instructions. This row decides whether those lines stay, change, or split in two.

opts.label: Replace the four lines with wording that fits any agent.
Keep the tool names, and put a condition in front of each.
Keep a Claude Code section, and add a section for other agents.
Leave them. Other agents skip what they cannot do.

dims.name: Whether the renderer is also an npm package
dims.question: Can somebody render a box without installing a skill?
dims.problem: The skills installer copies the renderer with the skill, so any agent that installs the skill can already run it. A package serves a different reader: somebody who keeps box files in a repository and wants a check in continuous integration, with no agent and no skill involved. A package also adds a second version number to keep in step with the plugin manifest.

opts.label: A package whose program is the renderer.
The same package, and it also exports the analyser for other programs.
No package. The renderer arrives with the skill and nowhere else.

dims.name: What the README leads with
dims.question: Three routes now exist. Which one does a stranger read first?
dims.problem: A reader can install the plugin, run the skills installer, or copy the directory by hand. The installer works for every agent, Claude Code included, and it is one line. The plugin updates itself and needs no third-party tool. A README that lists three routes before it explains the tool loses the reader. This row names the first route, not the only one.

opts.label: The skills installer first. It serves every agent in one line.
opts.src: measured: it installed from this repository

opts.label: The plugin first, as today. The installer comes second.
A short table. The reader finds their agent and reads one command.
List all three and name no first route.

dims.name: Where the skill directory sits
dims.question: Does the skill move nearer the top of the repository?
dims.problem: The skill lives four directories deep, inside the plugin that carries it. The installer finds it there, and so does Claude Code. A person who opens the repository on the web does not see a skill; they see a plugins folder. This row weighs a tooling fact against a human one, and the tooling fact is already settled. The first draft of this row assumed a repository at the top could hold only one skill. That is false: one plugin holds many skills under skills/<name>/.

opts.label: The repository is the plugin. Skills sit at skills/<name>/ and the marketplace stays.
opts.src: mattpocock/skills — marketplace.json and plugin.json side by side at the root, source "./"

opts.label: Leave it. Add links in the README so a person finds it.
opts.src: measured: the installer found it and copied every file

opts.label: A script writes a copy at the top of the repository, and the check keeps the two the same.
Drop the marketplace. One plugin, one skill, near the top.
Change nothing and add nothing. Move it if somebody reports they could not find it.

voice-neutral.why: Four lines carry all of it, so the edit is small. The slash command still works, because it comes from the frontmatter name, not from the prose.
notes: Measured: lines 27, 87, and 94 to 97 of SKILL.md. Nothing else names a Claude Code feature.
It loses a little precision for the Claude Code reader, who had exact instructions and now reads general ones.

voice-guard.why: Each line keeps its tool name and gains a condition, so a reader who has the tool gets the exact instruction.
notes: A conditional instruction is harder to read than a plain one, and there would be four of them.

voice-fork.why: Each reader gets text written for them, and neither has to skip anything.
notes: It doubles the part of the file most likely to change, and the two halves drift.

voice-keep.why: The none answer. The lines are few, and an agent that cannot follow one moves past it.
rel: The installer serves every agent, and the kept lines tell those readers to type a slash command their agent lacks.

pkg-bin.why: It serves the reader who has box files in a repository and wants the check in continuous integration, with no agent involved.
notes: It needs a package.json with a bin field at the repository root. Measured: npx cloned this repository and stopped at the missing file.
`eagle-eye` is taken on the registry by an unrelated package from 2022, so the name must be scoped or suffixed.
It adds a second version number beside the plugin manifest. Box 1's release row is where that cost lands.
Not chosen. The second version number was the cost, and no reader has asked for the check without an agent.

pkg-lib.why: The analyser is already a separate file with no dependencies. Exporting it lets other programs compute the findings.
notes: An exported function is a promise about its shape. Nobody has asked for it yet.

pkg-none.why: The none answer. The installer already delivers the renderer to every agent that installs the skill.
notes: The author picked this strawman. The skill says to give the reason to reject a strawman, or to pick it.
The reason it survives: the installer already delivers the renderer to every agent that installs the skill.
What it costs: a reader who keeps box files and runs no agent must clone the repository to get a check.

lead-skills.why: One line, every agent, and it worked against this repository unchanged.
notes: Measured: the installer found plugins/eagle-eye/skills/eagle-eye/SKILL.md, copied render.mjs, lib, examples and reference, and wrote a lock file naming that path.
It puts a third-party tool in front of the project's own install route.

lead-plugin.why: The route the project owns, and it updates itself. It needs no other tool.
notes: It serves Claude Code only, which is now the smaller half of the audience.

lead-split.why: A reader finds their own agent and reads one line, and never weighs a route that is not for them.
notes: A table is the first thing on the page, before the tool has been explained.

lead-none.why: The none answer. Describe three routes and let the reader choose.

layout-nested.why: Both install routes find the skill where it is. Links in the README fix the part the measurement does not cover.
notes: Measured: the installer's lock file records plugins/eagle-eye/skills/eagle-eye/SKILL.md and the copy ran from its new home.
The cost is human, not mechanical. Somebody browsing the repository sees a plugins folder, not a skill.
No longer chosen. The measurement still holds — both installers found the skill four levels down — but the nesting existed to serve a marketplace shape the repository no longer uses.

layout-mirror.why: A copy at the top of the repository is what a person sees first, and a check keeps it honest.
notes: Two copies of a 14 KB file in one repository. The check stops drift and does not stop confusion about which one to edit.

layout-single.why: A single-plugin repository needs no marketplace file, so the skill can sit one directory down.
notes: Sourced: a repository with one plugin installs without a marketplace file. code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-marketplaces.
It contradicts why this repository exists. Box 1 chose a marketplace so more skills can follow.
The premise was wrong. A root layout does not require dropping the marketplace, so this option was never the only way up.

layout-later.why: The later answer. No move, no links, and no cost until somebody is actually lost.
notes: Nobody reports a repository they gave up on. The signal this waits for does not arrive.

layout-root.why: One plugin, many skills, both manifests at the root. The shelf and the book carry different names.
notes: Sourced: mattpocock/skills ships marketplace.json and plugin.json together at the root, with the plugin source set to "./".
The Claude Code docs describe a marketplace and a plugin separately and never that pairing. A working repository is the evidence; claude plugin validate passes on it.
It costs plugin users the namespace: skills are invoked as /grimoire:eagle-eye. The installer route is unaffected.
This cell did not exist when the row was drawn. The row offered only nested or a single-skill repo, because the author believed a root layout meant dropping the marketplace.

suspected: layout-single conf scope-market — the target sits in box 1, so this box cannot draw the edge. It is the strongest argument against layout-single and it is recorded here instead.
pkg-bin conf layout-nested — a package root and a nested skill are unrelated; the package reads the renderer by path either way.
layout-single conf scope-market — recorded earlier as the strongest argument against a root layout. It was false: one plugin holds many skills, so growth never required the nesting.

weakly connected: voice-keep conf pkg-bin — the package reader runs the renderer with no agent and no skill involved, so the kept skill lines never reach them. Why: "A reader running the package outside any agent cannot act on advice about an in-app preview pane."

weakly connected: pkg-none conf lead-split — a table by agent has no row for a reader with no agent, and the pkg-none notes give that reader a route: clone the repository. Why: "A table by agent needs a row for the reader who wants only the renderer, and without a package that row has no command."

weakly connected: lead-none conf voice-neutral — neutral wording changes how the skill is used, not how the reader installed it, and lead-none still names all three routes. Why: "Neutral text assumes the reader arrived by a route the project did not name, so the README must name one."

weakly connected: layout-later conf lead-skills — the installer finds the skill four directories down, as measured, so the installer route does not need the README to show where the skill is. Why: "The first route sends a reader to this repository, so the README must show where the skill is."

presets.title: As recommended
presets.text: Neutral wording, a renderer package, the installer first, and the tree left alone because the measurement says it works.

presets.text: The strawman run. One edge rejects it, and it is argued, not measured.

presets.title: No package at all
presets.text: The installer already delivers the renderer. This asks what a package adds that it does not.

presets.title: One skill, no marketplace
presets.text: The repository was built to hold more skills. This is what dropping that plan would buy.
